objective.statement: Write and recognise the triads on the tonic, subdominant and dominant.
successCriteria: I know a triad is a root, a 3rd and a 5th.
I know the tonic, subdominant and dominant are chords I, IV and V.
I know minor keys use the harmonic minor for their triads.

explanation.text: A triad is three notes: a root, the note a 3rd above it, and the note a 5th above it. You can build a triad on any note of a scale. At Grade 4 you need the triads on three notes: the tonic (the 1st degree, chord I), the subdominant (the 4th, chord IV) and the dominant (the 5th, chord V). Together they are the primary triads of a key.

music.textAlternative: Three bars of 4/4, each with one chord: C, E and G; then F, A and C; then G, B and D.

explanation.caption: C major: tonic (I), subdominant (IV) and dominant (V).

explanation.text: In a major key all three primary triads are major triads: each has a major 3rd above its root. In a minor key the notes come from the harmonic minor. The tonic and subdominant triads are minor triads (a minor 3rd above the root), but the dominant is a major triad, because the harmonic minor raises the 7th to make the leading note, which is the 3rd of that chord.

music.textAlternative: Three bars of 4/4: C minor chords, the tonic C, E flat, G; the subdominant F, A flat, C; the dominant G, B, D.

explanation.caption: C minor: tonic (i), subdominant (iv) and dominant (V). The B natural is the raised leading note.

explanation.text: Roman numerals are shorthand for the same chords: I, IV and V. In this course you may write the numerals or the words (tonic, subdominant, dominant); capital letters only are accepted, so you will not lose marks for ignoring the small letters used for minor chords.
Triad = root, 3rd, 5th. I = tonic, IV = subdominant, V = dominant. In minor keys use the harmonic minor: V needs the raised 7th.

music.textAlternative: One bar of 4/4 with the dominant chord of C major: G, B and D.

steps: The dominant is the 5th degree: G.
Add the note a 3rd above (B) and a 5th above (D).
Together they are chord V of C major.
demonstration.textAlternative: The dominant triad of C major: G, B, D.

guided.prompt: Which notes make chord V (the dominant triad) of G♯ minor, using the harmonic minor scale?

G#-B-D#.reason: Those are the notes of chord I, the tonic. Chord V is built on the 5th degree.

D#-Fx-A.reason: The top note is the 5th above the root: count its distance in letters and semitones.

D#-Fx-Ax.reason: The top note is the 5th above the root: count its distance in letters and semitones.

hints: Chord V is built on degree 5 of the scale: that note, the one two letters above it and the one four letters above it.

mistakes.wrong-degree: Chord I is on degree 1, IV on 4 and V on 5.
mistakes.root-confused-with-bass: The lowest note isn't always the root. Stack the notes in 3rds to find it, then check the inversion.
mistakes.inversion-misread: Inversion depends on which note of the triad is in the bass: root (a), 3rd (b) or 5th (c).
mistakes.leading-note-not-raised: In a minor key the 3rd of chord V is the raised leading note.
mistakes.note-missing: One of the notes doesn't belong. A triad has a root, a 3rd and a 5th.
mistakes.wrong-third: Check the middle note: it must belong to the scale of the key (harmonic minor in minor keys).
mistakes.wrong-fifth: Count the fifth above the root in letters and in semitones.

feedback.fallback: Not quite. Find the root first, then the bass note.

provenance.authoredBy: Music Theory Path curriculum team (Brief 05, drafted with AI assistance; pending qualified teacher review)
provenance.notes: Original wording. Follows Grade 4 outcome 14 and First Steps Grade 4 section 10 (pp. 92-94, read in the PDF): primary triads, major triads in major keys, minor i and iv with major V in minor keys, the harmonic form. The book's extended-roman note (capital letters accepted) is followed. Chord I alone earns no Grade 4 credit (it is Grade 3 knowledge); the credit boundary requires chord IV or V or a naming question.
